newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIANS AMBIVALENT OVER CEAUSESCU HEIR DEATH.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIANS AMBIVALENT OVER CEAUSESCU HEIR DEATH.

text.p: Playboy, liberal? Romanians are undecided on how to remember Nicu Ceausescu, the youngest son of the late Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu who died in a Vienna hospital from acute liver disease on Thursday.
Nicu had been groomed to succeed his father, but that ended with the December 1989 uprising in which Ceausescu and his wife Elena were shot by a firing squad.

The playboy lifestyle of "the princeling" as he was dubbed during the communist era had contrasted with the poverty and food shortages that were the lot of most Romanians and epitomised the corruption of his father's rule.
"We'll be better off when Nicu takes over, because he'll gamble Romania at roulette tables in Las Vegas and the Americans will win us over," ran a popular communist-era joke.

But some remembered a less known, kinder side to the heir apparent. Leading commentator Ion Cristoiu said Nicu had been seen as a liberal by people of his own generation in contrast to his father's hardline supporters.
"His stand often put him on a collision course with the old guard around his father," he told Reuters.
Vienna hospital doctors said Nicu, 45, died "from bleeding of the oesophagus as a result of liver cirrhosis and viral inflammation of the liver".
Romanian private broadcasters flashed the news. State media kept their cover to a minimum.

"I don't have any feelings at all. I can't have feelings for people like the Ceausescus," said pensioner Jana Ioanid, echoing loathing deeply rooted among many Romanians, who still smart at the memory of Ceausescu's ruthless 24-year rule.
But despite his past reputation as a womaniser and gambler who squandered vast sums at gaming tables across the world, many first reactions in Romania were sympathetic.

"This is sad news, although it was expected given his grave illness. May God rest his soul, which was unjustly tormented," said pensioner Elisabeta Antim from Sibiu, Nicu's Transylvanian fiefdom where local people remember him for trying to oppose his father's severe economic belt-tightening.

Nicu's elder brother Valentin and his sister Zoe were affected by the news of his death in Vienna, where Nicu had been flown by friends last week after Romanian doctors said they lacked medical and surgical equipment to treat his condition.
"He didn't have a last wish...He had his friends...We hadn't seen each other often lately," Valentin said.
An Austrian magazine said friends of Nicu's had paid for his treatment in Vienna, reporting that $37,000 had been deposited with the Austrian embassy in Bucharest.
Nicu was arrested shortly before his parents' execution and charged with ordering troops to fire on protesters in Sibiu during the 1989 uprising. He always protested his innocence.
"He served out his sentence for illegal gun possession, and he (died) cleared of all other charges," said Valentin, who lobbied to have Nicu freed from jail in November 1992.
Friends will fly Nicu's body back home later this week. Relatives are making arrangements for his funeral in Bucharest, sources close to his family said. REUTER
